subject: chemistry
title: Rate equations and orders
key_idea: A rate equation links the rate to the concentrations of reactants: rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ. The orders m and n are found by experiment, not from the balanced equation. The rate constant k has units that depend on the overall order.

blocks.text: A rate equation shows how the rate depends on concentration. This section covers the terms and how to write one.

items.meaning: An equation that links the rate of reaction to the concentrations of the reactants.
The power to which the concentration of a reactant is raised in the rate equation.
The sum of the orders with respect to each reactant.
The constant in the rate equation. It is fixed at a given temperature.

blocks.label: Rate equation
where: m, n, orders with respect to A and B (0, 1 or 2)

items: The orders are found **by experiment**. They cannot be read from the coefficients in the balanced equation.
Only reactants (and sometimes catalysts) appear in the rate equation. Products usually do not.
A reactant with order 0 does not appear, because [A]⁰ = 1.
Orders come from experiments, not from the balanced equation.
Overall order is the sum of the individual orders.
The orders are 0, 1 or 2.

blocks.text: The order tells you how the rate changes when a concentration changes. This section covers the three orders.

diagram.alt: Choose the order and a factor by which the concentration is multiplied, and see how many times faster the rate becomes.

items: Order 1: rate is multiplied by the same factor.
Order 2: rate is multiplied by the factor squared.

blocks.text: The initial rate is measured in separate experiments with different starting concentrations. This section covers how to read the orders from the results.
Compare two experiments where only one concentration changes. The change in rate shows the order.

items: Experiments 1 and 2: [A] doubles and the rate doubles, so the reaction is first order in A.
Experiments 2 and 3: [B] doubles and the rate increases four times, so it is second order in B.
The rate equation is rate = k[A][B]². The overall order is 3.
Change one concentration at a time and compare the rates.
Rate × 2 for concentration × 2 means order 1; rate × 4 means order 2; no change means order 0.

sections.heading: The rate constant and its units

blocks.text: Once the rate equation is known, k is found by rearranging it. This section covers the calculation and the units.

items.text: Use any one experiment, such as experiment 1: k = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ ÷ (0.10 × 0.10²) = 0.20.
Put the units of rate and concentration into the rearranged equation and cancel.

diagram.alt: A calculation of a rate constant for a reaction that is first order in A and first order in B, with new numbers each time.
diagram.question: For a reaction with rate = k[A][B], the rate is {rate} mol/dm³/s when [A] = {a} mol/dm³ and [B] = {b} mol/dm³. Calculate k.

items: k is constant at a fixed temperature. A catalyst, or a rise in temperature, changes it.
A rise in temperature increases k, and so the rate. The Arrhenius equation (see its own note) explains how.
Rearrange the rate equation for k.
The units of k depend on the overall order.

checks.q: Define the term order of reaction.
checks.a: The power to which the concentration of a reactant is raised in the rate equation (how the rate depends on that concentration).

checks.q: The rate of a reaction is unchanged when the concentration of X doubles, and doubles when the concentration of Y doubles. Write the rate equation.
checks.a: rate = k[Y]. The order with respect to X is 0, so X does not appear.

checks.q: A reaction has rate = k[A]²[B]. When [A] = 0.20 mol/dm³ and [B] = 0.10 mol/dm³ the rate is 3.2 × 10⁻³ mol/dm³/s. Calculate k and give its units.

blocks.text: Know the terms in 5.1.1a, including half-life and rate-determining step, which are covered in the next notes.

items: Interpret initial-rate data to find the order for each reactant.
Integrated forms of rate equations are not required.

blocks.text: The terms for this course also include activation energy and heterogeneous and homogeneous catalysts. They are covered in earlier notes.

items: Be able to determine and use rate equations of the form rate = k[A]ᵐ[B]ⁿ.
Deduce an order from initial-rate data.

blocks.text: Know that k varies with temperature according to the Arrhenius equation, covered in its own note.

items: Explain the qualitative effect of temperature on k: k increases as T increases.
Equations and the gas constant are given when needed.

blocks.text: Be able to construct a rate equation and calculate an initial rate from concentration data.

items: Deduce orders from initial-rate data, from concentration–time graphs and by the half-life method.
Calculate k using the initial rates and the rate equation, or using k = 0.693 ÷ t½ for a first-order reaction.
